```{r validation-setup, include = FALSE}
vroot <- "."
source(file.path(vroot, "R", "report_helpers.R"))
res_dir <- file.path(vroot, "results")
rd <- function(f) { p <- file.path(res_dir, f); if (file.exists(p)) readRDS(p) else NULL }
v2 <- rd("01_component_equivalence.rds")
v3 <- rd("02_ga_comparison.rds")
v3b <- rd("02b_siga_comparison.rds")
v4 <- rd("03_radiant_case_study.rds")
v5 <- rd("04_simulation_tte.rds")
v6b <- rd("04_simulation_binary.rds")
v6c <- rd("04_simulation_continuous.rds")
rn5 <- rd("04_resample_number_tte_q100_bernoulli_legacydata.rds")
rn1 <- rd("04_resample_number_tte_s1_q100_legacydata.rds")
kt <- function(x, ...) knitr::kable(x, row.names = FALSE, ...)
ag5 <- if (!is.null(v5)) agreement(v5$summary)
agv <- function(m, what) ag5[[what]][ag5$metric == m]
sval <- function(s, metric, model, n, eta = 0.2, theta = 0.5, what = "value")
  s[[what]][s$metric == metric & s$model == model & s$n == n & s$eta == eta & s$theta == theta]
```

# Validation

The package was validated in six steps. The scripts are in the `validation/`
directory of the source repository. Published values are given in
parentheses.

## V1: unit tests

The test suite (`tests/testthat`, run by `R CMD check`) checks, among others,
that the subgroup decoding is correct for every predictor type including the
cases that failed in the original code, that the fast model fitters reproduce
`coxph()`, `glm()` and `lm()`, that the prescreening reproduces `anova()`,
that `update()` gives the same result as a new fit, that results are
identical with one and two cores, and that `siga_simulate(legacy = TRUE)`
reproduces the original simulation program.

## V2: equivalence with the original code

```{r, echo = FALSE}
if (!is.null(v2)) kt(data.frame(Check = names(v2),
                               Result = ifelse(vapply(v2, `[[`, TRUE, "ok"), "pass", "FAIL"),
                               Detail = vapply(v2, `[[`, "", "detail")))
```

The genetic algorithm of the package reproduces the original implementation
exactly: with the same random seed and objective values, the best objective
value of each of 50 generations is identical for 5 seeds (check d).

## V3: comparison with the original code

**One genetic algorithm run.** On 50 simulated B3 datasets ($n = 300$,
original simulation program) one single-population genetic algorithm run of
the original `SIGA.tte()` and of the package were applied to the same 10
prescreened candidates. Both best subgroups were scored with the same
criterion, the one-sided interaction p-value. The searches reach similar
objective values. Both are lower than that of the true subgroup, which
illustrates why a single search overfits and the resampling scheme is needed.
The package finds subgroups defined by the true biomarkers $x_4$ and $x_5$
more often, because subgroups with a single binary condition such as
$x_5 = 1$ were unreachable in the original code. It is about 35 times faster.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
if (!is.null(v3)) kt(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("datasets", "median log10 p of best subgroup", "best subgroup contains x4 and x5",
               "best subgroup uses exactly x4 and x5", "mean time per run (s)"),
  Original = c(nrow(v3), f3(median(log10(v3$p_old)), 2), sum(v3$all_old), sum(v3$exact_old),
               f3(mean(v3$time_old), 1)),
  Package = c(nrow(v3), f3(median(log10(v3$p_new)), 2), sum(v3$all_new), sum(v3$exact_new),
              f3(mean(v3$time_new), 2))))
```

**The complete procedure.** The original `SIGA()` function and `siga()` were
applied with the same settings (5 sub-populations and 10 resamples with
Bernoulli sampling, $\eta = 0.2$, $\theta = 0.5$) to the same datasets of
models B1 ($n = 300$) and B4 ($n = 600$) generated with the original
simulation program (script `02b_siga_comparison.R`).

```{r, echo = FALSE}
if (!is.null(v3b)) {
  a <- v3b$summary
  kt(data.frame(Model = a$model, Code = a$method, Datasets = a$datasets,
                `Subgroup found` = f3(a$found, 2), `Same decision` = f3(a$same_decision, 2),
                `Held-out / overall HR` = f3(a$test_over_overall, 2),
                `Variables per rule` = f3(a$vars_per_rule, 2),
                `Lowest frequency, predictive` = f3(a$min_freq_predictive, 2),
                `Highest frequency, noise` = f3(a$max_freq_noise, 2),
                `Final rule: all predictive` = f3(a$all, 2),
                `Final rule: exactly the predictive` = f3(a$exact, 2), check.names = FALSE),
     caption = paste("Original code versus package on the same datasets: proportion of datasets with a",
                     "subgroup and with the same decision as the other code; means over the datasets of the",
                     "held-out / overall hazard ratio and the number of variables of the resampled",
                     "subgroups, of the lowest selection frequency of a predictive biomarker and the",
                     "highest of a noise variable; proportion of datasets whose final rule uses all /",
                     "exactly the predictive biomarkers"))
}
```

The two codes make the same decision (subgroup or no subgroup) in 31 of the
32 datasets. They give similar held-out hazard ratios, numbers of variables
per rule and selection frequencies, and both final rules contain $x_4$ in 22
of the 24 B1 datasets. In this run the final rule of the package contained an
additional noise variable more often (exactly $x_4$: 11 versus 17 datasets;
7 versus 1 discordant datasets, exact binomial $p = 0.07$). This is resampling
variation. With three further seeds on the same datasets the package's final
rule is exactly $x_4$ in 69% of the runs (71%, 71% and 67% for the three
seeds), about the same as the original code (71%). In B4 both codes often miss
one of the three biomarkers.

## V4: RADIANT case study

The case study of the paper (973 patients, 21 predictors, disease-free
survival) was repeated with the settings of the paper ($k = 10$, $q = 100$,
$\eta = 0.25$, $\theta = 0.7$) and three seeds: with the package defaults
otherwise (`default`: five sub-populations per resample, exactly 63.2% of the
patients), with the sampling of the original code (`bernoulli`) and with one
sub-population per resample as described in the paper (`one_subpop`).
`default_q10` uses the package defaults including $q = 10$ (ten seeds). The
RADIANT data are not part of the package.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
if (!is.null(v4)) kt(v4$original, caption = "Original code (stored result)", digits = 3)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
if (!is.null(v4)) kt(v4$runs[c("config", "seed", "n_resample", "mean_test_hr", "freq_ihc_prop",
                               "freq_ihc_intense", "subgroup", "subgroup_eta0.2_theta0.5")], digits = 3,
                     caption = paste("SIGA package: mean test-set hazard ratio, selection frequencies of",
                                     "EGFR_IHC_PROP and EGFR_IHC_INTENSE, subgroup with eta = 0.25 /",
                                     "theta = 0.7 and with eta = 0.2 / theta = 0.5"))
```

The overall hazard ratio is 0.945, as in the original analysis. That analysis
is itself borderline: in its stored result EGFR_IHC_INTENSE is used by exactly
70 of the 100 resampled subgroups (EGFR_IHC_PROP by 85), so $\theta = 0.7$ is
just reached. With $q = 100$ and five sub-populations per resample the
package gives similar mean test-set hazard ratios (0.67 to 0.71; original 0.70) and
selection frequencies (EGFR_IHC_PROP 0.80 to 0.85, EGFR_IHC_INTENSE 0.65 to
0.73), so whether EGFR_IHC_INTENSE reaches 70% depends on the seed. With the
defaults the final rule is the published one (hazard ratio 0.51 in the
subgroup) for two of the three seeds and EGFR_IHC_PROP $\le 25$ (0.55) for
the third. With the sampling of the original code EGFR_IHC_INTENSE stays at
65% to 68%. For seed 1 the mean test-set hazard ratio (0.711) is also just
above the threshold $(1 - 0.25) \times 0.945 = 0.709$. With one
sub-population per resample neither biomarker reaches 70% (55% to 67%), so no
subgroup is found, as expected from V5. With $\eta = 0.2$ and $\theta = 0.5$
all nine runs with $q = 100$ give the published subgroup.

With $q = 10$ the mean test-set hazard ratio varies between 0.53 and 0.81
over the ten seeds. At $\eta = 0.25$ and $\theta = 0.7$ five seeds give a
subgroup, the published one twice. At $\eta = 0.2$ and $\theta = 0.5$ eight
do. All eight contain EGFR_IHC_INTENSE $\le 1$ and EGFR_IHC_PROP $\le 60$ or
70, and three have no further conditions.

## V5: simulation study of the paper

The simulation study of section 3 of the paper was repeated with the package
defaults (10 resamples with five sub-populations each, exactly 63.2% of the
patients per resample) and the settings of the paper otherwise ($k = 10$,
$m = 50$, $MaxG = 50$, $s = 5$, $GGAP = 0.9$, $MinS = 10\%$), with 100 trials
per scenario (the paper used 1000). The observed time is $\min(T, C)$, as
described in the paper. In every trial the nine combinations of $\eta$ and
$\theta$ are evaluated from the same resampling with `update()`.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
if (!is.null(ag5)) kt(data.frame(Metric = ag5$metric, Cells = ag5$cells, Package = f3(ag5$package),
                                 Paper = f3(ag5$paper), `Within 2 SE` = ag5$within_2se, check.names = FALSE),
                      caption = paste("Agreement with Tables 3 to 6 of the paper: means over the cells and",
                                      "number of cells within two Monte Carlo standard errors"))
```

The false discovery rates agree with Table 3 of the paper: 35 of the 36 cells
are within two Monte Carlo standard errors. At $\theta = 0.5$, averaged over
the four null scenarios, they are 0.087, 0.058 and 0.028 for $\eta = 0.15$,
0.2 and 0.25 (paper 0.109, 0.061 and 0.032), and they decrease with $\theta$
as in the paper. When a subgroup is found, it uses at least one predictive
biomarker in 97% of the trials (paper 99.7%). Its hazard ratio in the test set
$L_2$ agrees with the paper (0.32 versus 0.33 on average), and sensitivity,
specificity and AUC are similar on average (AUC 0.90 versus 0.89). The final
rules contain a noise variable more often (`p_exact`). They also miss a
predictive biomarker of models B3 and B4 more often (`p_all`), and their hazard
ratios in the training set $L_1$ are lower than published. These differences
are discussed at the end of this section.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
if (!is.null(v5)) kt(table3(v5$summary),
                     caption = "False subgroup discovery rates (Table 3), package (paper)")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
if (!is.null(v5)) kt(table_discovery(v5$summary),
                     caption = "Subgroup discovery rates in models B1 to B4 (not reported in the paper)")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
if (!is.null(v5)) for (n in c(300, 600)) {
  print(kt(table_metrics(v5$summary, c("p_one", "p_all", "p_exact"), n),
           caption = sprintf("Probability of selecting the predictive biomarkers (Table 4), n = %d, package (paper)", n)))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
if (!is.null(v5)) for (n in c(300, 600)) {
  print(kt(table_metrics(v5$summary, c("se", "sp", "auc"), n, d = 2),
           caption = sprintf("Sensitivity, specificity and AUC (Table 5), n = %d, package (paper)", n)))
  cat("\n\n")
  print(kt(table_metrics(v5$summary, c("prop_L2", "est_L1", "est_L2", "rel_bias"), n, d = 2),
           caption = sprintf("Subgroup proportion and hazard ratios in L1 and L2 (Table 6), n = %d, package (paper)", n)))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

### Resampling settings and data generation

The agreement with the paper depends on the resampling settings and on how the
data are generated. The following runs used the same datasets (seeds) as far
as the data generator is the same.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
cfg <- c(tte = "package defaults: s = 5, q = 10, exact; min(T, C)",
         tte_bernoulli = "s = 5, q = 10, Bernoulli; min(T, C)",
         tte_bernoulli_legacydata = "s = 5, q = 10, Bernoulli; original program",
         tte_s1_legacydata = "s = 1, q = 10, exact; original program",
         tte_s1_q100_legacydata = "s = 1, q = 100, exact; original program")
ct <- config_table(cfg, res_dir)
if (!is.null(ct)) kt(ct, caption = paste(
  "Resampling settings (s sub-populations per resample, q resamples, exact or Bernoulli sampling)",
  "and data generator: trials per scenario, means over the cells of Tables 3 to 6 (in brackets the",
  "share of cells within two Monte Carlo standard errors of the paper) and discovery rates at",
  "eta = 0.2, theta = 0.5 / 0.9"))
```

Exact and Bernoulli sampling give similar results, and so do the two data
generators (first three rows; runs with 50 trials per scenario have larger
Monte Carlo errors). One sub-population per resample, as described in the
paper, finds the subgroups less often. B1 ($n = 300$) is then found in 68% of
the trials at $\theta = 0.5$ and in 9% at $\theta = 0.9$, against 88% and 76%
with five sub-populations. A single search in a resample more often ends at a
poor subgroup, so the predictive biomarkers are selected in fewer resamples.
With $q = 100$ resamples (last row) false discoveries are rare (0.3%) and
almost no subgroup is found at $\theta = 0.9$ (next section).

### Number of resamples

The paper recommends $q = 100$ resamples, whereas the original `SIGA()`
function used 10 by default. Runs with $q = 100$ that store all resamples
show which decisions fewer resamples would have given: the first $q$
resamples are exactly those of a run with `n_resample = q` and the same seed,
and averaging over random subsets of $q$ resamples gives the expected rate.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
if (!is.null(rn5)) {
  x <- rn5[rn5$theta == 0.5 & rn5$n == 300, ]
  w <- reshape(x[c("model", "eta", "q", "random")], idvar = c("model", "eta"), timevar = "q",
               direction = "wide")
  w <- w[order(w$model, w$eta), ]
  kt(data.frame(Model = w$model, eta = w$eta, `q = 10` = f3(w$random.10), `q = 20` = f3(w$random.20),
                `q = 50` = f3(w$random.50), `q = 100` = f3(w$random.100), check.names = FALSE),
     caption = paste("Expected false discovery rate with q resamples, theta = 0.5, n = 300 (50 datasets",
                     "per model; 5 sub-populations, Bernoulli sampling, original simulation program).",
                     "Paper (eta = 0.15 / 0.2 / 0.25): A1 0.094 / 0.059 / 0.036, A2 0.099 / 0.060 / 0.034"))
}
```

Under the null hypothesis the held-out hazard ratio of a subgroup found in a
resample is on average higher than the overall hazard ratio, because the
subgroup was selected in the training part. In the V5 trials it is 18% to 21%
higher for $n = 300$ and 8% to 9% higher for $n = 600$. A false discovery
therefore requires the mean of the $q$ held-out ratios to be low by chance,
which becomes unlikely for large $q$. With $q = 10$ the expected false
discovery rates of A1 are close to the published ones (0.101, 0.060 and 0.030
for $\eta = 0.15$, 0.2 and 0.25). Those of A2 are lower on data from the
original simulation program but agree with the paper under proper censoring
(Table 3 above). With $q = 100$ the rates are 0 for $\eta \ge 0.15$. To keep
the false discovery rate near 5% with $q = 100$, $\eta$ must be about 0.05 to
0.10: the rates are then 0.06 and 0.02 for A1 and 0.02 and 0 for A2. The
defaults ($q = 10$, $\eta = 0.2$) correspond to the calibration of the
published simulations. With only 10 resamples the decision depends on the
random resamples, so a borderline result should be repeated with a few seeds.

### Differences from the published results

* **Noise variables in the final rule.** At $\theta = 0.5$ the final rule
  more often contains a noise variable besides the predictive biomarkers
  (B1, $n = 300$: `p_exact` 0.71 versus 0.99). With 10 resamples a noise
  variable needs to appear in only 5 of them to be selected. At
  $\theta = 0.7$ the final rules of B1 and B2 are exact in 93% of the trials.
  On the same data the original code also selects noise variables (V3: the
  final rule is exactly $x_4$ in 17 of the 22 B1 datasets with a subgroup).
* **Biomarkers of B3 and B4.** `p_all` is lower, mainly at
  $\theta \ge 0.7$ (B4, $n = 600$, $\theta = 0.7$: 0.24 versus 0.68). One of
  the biomarkers is often selected in fewer than 70% of the resamples. In B4
  this is mostly $x_1$, whose condition $x_1 < 0.5$ excludes only 31% of the
  patients; in B3 with $n = 300$ it is mostly the binary $x_5$. The original
  code is equally low on the same data (V3).
* **Subgroup size in B4, $n = 300$.** The published subgroups contain 64% of
  the patients and have a hazard ratio of 0.59 in $L_2$. The package's contain
  30% and have 0.37. For $n = 600$ the two are closer: 19% and 0.17 published,
  24% and 0.26 with the package.
* **Hazard ratio in the training set.** In $L_1$, the data in which the final
  subgroup was found, its hazard ratio is lower than in $L_2$, as expected
  after selection. The relative bias is −0.18 on average, and −0.43 for B3 with
  $n = 300$. The published estimates in $L_1$ are close to those in $L_2$
  (relative bias 0.02 on average). The estimates in $L_2$ agree with the
  paper.

## V6: binary and continuous endpoints

The binary and continuous versions of the six models (`siga_simulate()`,
section "Binary and continuous endpoints") were run with the package defaults
and 100 trials per scenario. The paper has no results for these endpoints.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
for (v in list(list(v6b, "binary"), list(v6c, "continuous"))) if (!is.null(v[[1]])) {
  print(kt(table3(v[[1]]$summary, with_paper = FALSE),
           caption = sprintf("False subgroup discovery rates, %s endpoint", v[[2]])))
  cat("\n\n")
  print(kt(table_discovery(v[[1]]$summary), caption = sprintf("Discovery rates, %s endpoint", v[[2]])))
  cat("\n\n")
  for (n in c(300, 600)) {
    print(kt(table_metrics(v[[1]]$summary, c("p_one", "p_all", "p_exact"), n, with_paper = FALSE),
             caption = sprintf("Probability of selecting the predictive biomarkers, %s endpoint, n = %d",
                               v[[2]], n)))
    cat("\n\n")
  }
}
```

With $\eta = 0.2$ and $\theta = 0.5$ the false discovery rate for continuous
endpoints, averaged over the four null scenarios, is 0.055, as for
time-to-event endpoints (0.058, V5). For binary endpoints it is 0.085 (Monte
Carlo standard error 0.014), and a stricter $\theta$ removes few of these
false discoveries: at $\theta = 0.7$ the rate is 0.077, against 0.028 for
time-to-event and 0.037 for continuous endpoints. In 31 of the 34 binary null
trials that passed the $\eta$ rule a predictor was selected in at least 70% of
the resamples (time-to-event: 11 of 23). With $\eta = 0.25$ the binary rates
are 0.058 and 0.052, about the rate of the defaults for time-to-event
endpoints, so $\eta = 0.25$ is the default for binary endpoints.

The subgroups are found less often than for time-to-event endpoints. B1 is
found in 61% (binary) and 44% (continuous) of the trials with $n = 300$,
against 88%. With $n = 600$ it is found in 90% and 87% (100%), and B2 to B4 in
40% to 51% (binary) and 37% to 52% (continuous), against 81% to 84%. The
linear predictors are the same for all endpoints, but a binary or continuous
outcome carries less information on the treatment effect than an event time
with 30% censoring: in the null trials the logarithms of the held-out ratios
vary about twice as much (variance about 0.6 against 0.34 for $n = 300$).
When a subgroup is found it uses a predictive biomarker in most trials (B1:
95% to 100%). At $\theta = 0.7$ the final rule of B1 is exactly $x_4$ in 90%
to 92% of the trials with a subgroup for both endpoints (time-to-event 94% to
96%). The final rules of B3 and B4 contain all predictive biomarkers less
often than for time-to-event endpoints (with $n = 600$ and $\theta = 0.5$:
43% and 5% for binary, 46% and 22% for continuous, 79% and 48% for
time-to-event endpoints).

The treatment effect of the final subgroup in $L_1$, the data in which it was
found, overestimates that in $L_2$ more than for time-to-event endpoints,
particularly for odds ratios. In B1 with $n = 300$ the odds ratio is 14.0 in
$L_1$ and 6.1 in $L_2$ (true value $e^2 = 7.4$ in the B1 subgroup), and the
mean difference is 2.6 and 1.9 (true value 2). `siga_cv()` estimates the
effect in new patients by cross-validation of the whole procedure. Earlier
runs with one sub-population and 100 resamples (30 trials per scenario) found
B1 in 20% and 70% of the binary trials, with almost no false discoveries, as
for time-to-event endpoints (V5).
